one_liner: Embeddable RISC-V sandbox for game scripting; 2 ns host-to-guest calls versus about 150 ns into LuaJIT, mixed on compute.
what_it_does: libriscv is a C++ userspace RISC-V emulator (RV32/RV64 GCVB, RVA23U64 profile) meant to be embedded in a host program as a scripting sandbox: you compile scripts in C, C++, Rust, Nim or Zig with a RISC-V cross-compiler and load the ELF into a riscv::Machine. The host calls exported guest functions with machine.vmcall("name", args...) or prepared calls, and the guest calls the host through custom system calls or string-keyed 'dynamic calls'; memory, stack and instruction limits bound each call. Execution modes are an interpreter (portable, the production-safe default), libtcc-based binary translation at load time, or ahead-of-time translated C99 that can be compiled into the final build. It is not a Lua or LuaJIT replacement at the language level: you change the scripting language and toolchain.
how_it_is_fast: Call latency is low because a vmcall only writes argument registers and jumps into an already-decoded execute segment, returning through a dedicated fast-exit address, with no stack marshalling through a dynamic-language C API. Common host operations (memcpy, memset, string handling) are 'accelerated system calls' that run natively on the host. Throughput comes from a computed-goto threaded interpreter over pre-decoded instructions, a flat read-write memory arena that avoids page-table lookups, and binary translation of RISC-V basic blocks into C that libtcc (JIT-like, 2-5x over the interpreter) or a full optimising compiler (ahead of time) turns into native code.
when_to_use: Game or engine scripting where the host makes many short calls into scripts per frame and per-call latency (tens of ns versus hundreds) matters more than peak compute.
Sandboxing untrusted, precompiled code from compiled languages with hard instruction and memory limits, pause/resume, preemption and serialisable VM state.
Platforms that forbid executable memory (consoles, iOS-style mobile): ship the interpreter plus an embedded ahead-of-time translation compiled into the binary.
Many short-lived instances: execute segments are shared between machines and copy-on-write forking supports ephemeral per-request VMs.
when_not_to_use: Compute-heavy scripts in production: SECURITY.md says not to use binary translation in production yet, and the interpreter runs CoreMark at about 3,559 iterations/s versus 41,382 native on a Ryzen 7950X (under 10%, derived from page data); LuaJIT also wins taylor(1K) by 2.6x even against libtcc translation.
You want a dynamic, hot-reloadable scripting language for designers: scripts need a RISC-V cross-compiler (GCC 10-14 riscv64-linux-gnu, or GCC 16+ for -march=rva23u64) and a rebuild of the ELF.

Running general Linux programs that need filesystem or socket access in a hostile setting: those Linux system call emulations are flagged not for production, and Linux syscall coverage is an explicit non-goal.
Bulk memory work done in guest code: the same gist shows guest-side naive memcpy at 586 ns versus 87 ns for LuaJIT; only the host-accelerated syscall variants win.
Go guests or Zig-built C++ guests: open issues report high memory footprint with Go (#264) and C++ exceptions failing on Zig toolchains (#267).

integration.dependencies: none for the interpreter; libtcc (fetched by CMake FetchContent from the fwsGonzo/tinycc 'mob' branch when RISCV_LIBTCC=ON, the default with binary translation) and libdl for translation; optional asmjit backend (experimental); a RISC-V cross-compiler for guest programs
integration.min_toolchain: CMake 3.5+; C++20 (lib/CMakeLists.txt sets cxx_std_20 PUBLIC although the README says C++17 or later); GCC or Clang for the computed-goto threaded dispatch (other compilers fall back to switch dispatch); Clang-cl on Windows
integration.platforms: any host for the interpreter (Linux, FreeBSD, macOS, Windows via Clang-cl or MinGW, Android, WebAssembly via Emscripten); libtcc translation on x86-64 and arm64 hosts; guests RV32GCVB, RV64GCVB (RVA23U64), experimental RV128G
integration.thread_safety: A Machine is not documented as safe for concurrent use (use one per thread or fork per request); sharing execute segments between machines and live-patching background translations are documented as thread-safe.

gotchas: The LuaJIT comparison numbers come from libtcc binary translation and the README's CoreMark 38,224 vs 41,382 native (92%) from an embedded full translation of GCC 13.2 -O3 guest code, yet SECURITY.md says 'Do not use binary translation in production at this time'. In the same CoreMark gist, libtcc mode reaches 18,294 (44% of native), the sandboxed mode with instruction counting 34,473 (83%) and the interpreter 3,559.

The LuaJIT gist mostly measures call and syscall latency of tiny functions, with call overhead subtracted on both sides and LuaJIT driven through the Lua C API. Its memcpy and memset wins (18 vs 87 ns, 15 vs 67 ns) are host-native accelerated syscalls; guest-code naive memcpy (586 ns) and memset (188 ns) lose to LuaJIT by 6.7x and 2.8x. No CPU, compiler, flags or LuaJIT version is given, and no harness source is linked (not found in rvscript's engine, scripts or programs directories at HEAD).

The two gists disagree: the interpreted gist (June 2025) reports integer math 3 ns and syscall 3 ns, faster than the binary-translated gist (October 2025: 6 ns and 10 ns), so they were not run on the same build or machine. The interpreted run also loses fib(40) to LuaJIT (156 vs 60 ns) and ties sieve(10M) (133 vs 131 ms).

The headline 2-3 ns call latency needs a custom fast-exit function: open issue #311 reports the default exit address is created and destroyed on every call, giving much higher call latency unless the host sets memory.set_exit_address() to a guest function. Embedded translations are keyed by a hash of the program and libriscv configuration, and any mismatch silently falls back to the interpreter.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick libriscv over rv32emu, rv8 or RVVM when you embed a sandbox in your own application and care about host-to-guest call latency, instruction limits and pause/resume rather than raw emulation throughput of whole programs; pick rv32emu (tiered JIT) or RVVM when you want to run complete RV32 programs or full systems as fast as possible, or Blink/Box64 when the guest ISA is x86-64 rather than RISC-V.
verified_claims_summary: In the author's gist (October 2025, medians of 200x1200 samples, call overhead subtracted on both sides, CPU, compiler and LuaJIT version not stated), libriscv with libtcc binary translation calls a guest function in 2 ns versus 156 ns for LuaJIT and handles a zero-argument syscall in 10 versus 174 ns, but compute rows are mixed: sieve(10M) 80 versus 123 ms (about 1.5x), fib(40) tied at 66 ns, taylor(1K) 2,234 versus 858 ns (LuaJIT 2.6x faster). The README's 92%-of-native CoreMark (38,224 vs 41,382 on a Ryzen 7950X) is from ahead-of-time embedded binary translation, not from the libtcc mode used for the LuaJIT comparison.
status_note: Actively developed (last commit 2026-09-30, about 3,200 commits, 1.1k stars, BSD-3-Clause; the same organisation maintains godot-sandbox) by essentially one author; the interpreter is the production-safe path, while the binary translation modes behind most of the speed claims are still marked not for production in SECURITY.md.
